My husband stopped snoring on a Tuesday. I know, because I was awake for all of it, waiting for the sound the way you wait for a dripping tap.

For years the routine was: elbow, roll over, five quiet minutes, start again. I'd moved to the spare room twice that month.

The strips didn't fix it. The spray definitely didn't.

What changed was his pillow, of all things. A contoured one that keeps his head and neck lined up instead of tipped back — because when the head tips, the airway narrows, and that's the noise.

Tuesday night: silence. I actually checked he was breathing.

It's been weeks now. He says his neck feels better. I just care that the bedroom is quiet and I'm sleeping in it.

If you — or the person next to you — rattles the windows at 2am, look at what the pillow is doing to their posture first. 👇

At 58 I assumed waking up with a stiff neck was just part of getting older.

Every morning started the same. Sit up slowly. Wince. Rub the right side of my neck through the first coffee.

I'd tried the expensive memory foam one. Flat in a month. I'd tried sleeping on two pillows. Worse.

Then my physio-obsessed daughter said something I couldn't unhear: "You spend eight hours a night with your head at an angle you'd never hold awake."

The fix wasn't stretches. It was a pillow shaped to hold my neck level — a butterfly contour with support wings, so my head sits in line instead of sinking.

The first night felt strange, like it was doing the holding for me. By the end of the week I was waking before the alarm with a loose neck and no headache.

I'm not saying it's magic. I'm saying my old pillow was the problem, and I'd spent two years blaming my age.

If your mornings start with a wince, it's worth seeing how the shape works. 👇

I did it three times. Each one arrived plump, lasted a few weeks, then packed down into the same shapeless slab. And every morning my neck paid for it.

Here's the part nobody tells you: an ordinary pillow has no structure. Your head sinks until your spine spends the night bent sideways. Eight hours. Every night. You can't out-stretch that in the morning.

What I ended up with isn't a softer pillow or a bigger one. It's a shaped one — a butterfly contour in high-density foam that decides the position for you. Neck level. Shoulders relaxed. Arms with somewhere to go.

And it doesn't pack flat, because the shape is the whole point.

I stopped waking up more tired than I went to bed. That's the entire review.

If you've bought three pillows in two years: stop replacing, start supporting. See how the shape works. 👇

ad_creative_bodies:
💔 There is a kind of homesickness that has nothing to do with a place.

It is being homesick for a person you love. A person you would give anything to see again, hear again, sit beside again.

After her husband died, a friend once told me that was the closest word she could find for what she felt.

Homesick.

She missed the sound of him walking through the house. The way he would say her name. The ordinary conversations that never seemed important until there were no more of them.

She missed having someone to tell the little things to.

She missed looking across the room and knowing he was there.

She even missed the things that used to drive her crazy. Funny how grief can make you long for the shoes left in the wrong place or the television turned up too loud.

There were days when she would have given anything to be annoyed by him one more time.

And I think that is one of the strangest parts of grief.

You can be surrounded by people who love you. You can laugh. You can go to dinner. You can have moments when life actually feels good again.

And still, underneath all of it, there can be this ache for one particular person.

Because there is no substitute for the person you are missing.

Sometimes you are simply homesick for someone you will never see again in this lifetime.

That is one of the reasons I wrote When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up.

I wanted to put words around the parts of grief that are so hard to explain. The missing. The longing. The strange moments when life looks completely normal from the outside while inside you are thinking, “I just want my person back.”

If you know this kind of homesickness, this book was written for you.

📖 Get your copy of When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up today and find words for some of the things you may have been carrying quietly on your own.

👉 Tap “Order Now” to get your copy today.

ad_creative_bodies:
💔 Grief really can feel like being sad every minute of every day.  Not necessarily crying every minute.

Not necessarily falling apart every minute.

But carrying a sadness that seems to sit underneath everything.

You can be driving to the store, answering an email, folding laundry, talking to someone, even laughing at something funny...

and the grief is still there.

There is this strange melancholy that follows you around.

Sometimes it is loud.

Sometimes it is barely noticeable.

Sometimes you are having what looks like a perfectly normal day and then, out of nowhere, you remember again.

They are gone.

And for a second, it can feel like you are learning it all over again.

That is one of the things people do not always understand about grief.

You can function and still be deeply sad.

You can smile and still miss them terribly.

You can have a good moment and still feel the ache underneath it.

You can keep living your life while also wishing with everything in you that one enormous part of it had never changed.

And sometimes that is exhausting.

Because there is no real “off” switch.

You do not clock out of grief at five o’clock.

You do not leave it in the car when you walk into the grocery store.

You do not put it away because everyone around you seems ready for things to feel normal again.

Grief comes with you.

That is one of the reasons I wrote When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up.

I wanted to talk about the parts of grief that can be so hard to explain to other people. The sadness that lingers. The thoughts that keep coming back. The strange experience of continuing to live your life while missing someone every single day.

If grief seems to be following you everywhere right now, this book was written for you.

📖 Get your copy of When Grief & Loss Won’t Shut Up today and let it help put words around some of what you have been carrying.

I was 73, and I thought nothing could surprise me anymore. But nothing in my long, complicated, beautiful life prepared me for the humiliation I felt that Sunday afternoon at my great-grandson's christening.
It was supposed to be a perfect day. And it was. For everyone else. Friends, family, laughter, warm hugs. I stood near the front with my heart full as my grandson walked up holding the baby.
"Mom," he said, smiling proudly. "Come say hi to little James."
Everyone turned toward me. Waiting. Expecting. Smiling. I opened my mouth to greet the baby and nothing came out. His name, a name I had heard a hundred times over the past month, was gone. Vanished.
I stared at his sweet little face and my mind went blank. Dead air. My throat tightened. My chest squeezed. Heat crawled up my cheeks. And as I looked around, I watched their expressions shift. Confusion. Concern. Then pity.
And pity cuts deeper than any insult. It wounds the soul. 💔
The whispers started. Not out loud but I felt them. "Poor woman… she's slipping." "That's what happens at her age."
I wanted to disappear. That moment cracked something inside me.
That night I couldn't sleep. I stared at the ceiling, tears sliding quietly down my face. My name is Ruth Calloway. I live in a small town just outside of Greenville, South Carolina. And I will never forget that night. The night I felt myself fading. Slowly becoming invisible to the people I loved. Losing my mind one forgotten moment at a time. 😢
The senior moments kept multiplying. I'd forget where I put my keys. Why I walked into a room. Full conversations I'd had hours earlier. The fog rolled in thick and heavy, making it impossible to think straight. Even reading became difficult. Holding onto a thought felt like trying to carry water in my hands. I was terrified.
But I hid it. Smiled through it. Pretended everything was fine. I didn't want anyone to worry. But my daughter Rebecca saw right through me. She never said anything directly, but her eyes did. That quiet fear. That silent sadness.
And the worst part? I saw doubt in my granddaughter's eyes too. Like she wasn't sure she could trust me alone with the baby. 😞
That shattered me.
Meanwhile the bills kept rising. Groceries, utilities, gas, medications. Everything cost more. My savings were dwindling. Social Security wasn't enough. I felt useless. Small. Afraid.
Until one day Rebecca said:
"Mom, the couple who owns the company I work for is looking for a part-time nanny. Just a few days a week. Their newborn son. They're very private, very kind, and I mentioned you."
"Me?" I blinked. "A nanny?"
"They want someone mature," she said softly. "Gentle. Trustworthy. Someone like you."
I wanted to say no. I was scared I'd forget something important. That I'd fail. But stronger than that fear was my need to feel needed again.
So I said yes.
A few days later I stood in front of a beautiful home just outside of town. Not flashy. But intentional. Warm wood everywhere. Books lining the hallways. A garden that someone clearly loved. The kind of place that felt lived in, not just decorated.
The woman who opened the door was tall, graceful, elegant without trying. But her eyes were soft.
"You must be Ruth," she said. "I'm Claudette. Please come in."
She was in her early sixties maybe. But there was something about her. Sharp. Present. Grounded. She showed me around, introduced me to baby Eli, walked me through every detail. Feeding times, nap routines, the lullaby playlist. Then just as I picked up my purse to leave she said something that stopped me.
"This job isn't just about the baby."
I frowned. "What do you mean?"
"It's about you too," she said calmly. "Most people think aging means decline. It doesn't. Not if you know what's really happening inside your brain."
I didn't know what to say. So I smiled politely and left. But her words stayed with me.
The next week I started. Nervous but hopeful. Claudette treated me not like an employee but like a welcomed guest. Every conversation felt intentional. Gentle. Awake.
One evening after Eli fell asleep I found her in the library. A fire glowed behind her. She sat in an armchair, eyes closed, wearing a pair of sleek headphones.
"Sorry," I whispered. "Didn't mean to interrupt."
She opened her eyes slowly, smiling.
"You didn't. I'm just tuning in. Would you like to try?"
"What is it?" I asked.
She paused for a moment. Then she said something I wasn't expecting.
"Ruth, do you know why some people stay sharp into their eighties and nineties while others fade? It's not luck. It's not genetics. There's something in your brain right now, a protein that researchers have been studying quietly for years. Harvard. The National Institute of Aging. They call it the memory protein. When it's active, your mind is clear, your memory works, your thinking is sharp."
I felt my hands go still in my lap. She kept going.
"But after a certain age, especially after stress and grief, it goes dormant. And nobody tells you. Because the people who profit from you staying foggy and medicated don't want you to know it can be reactivated."
She held out another pair of headphones.
"This is something that was developed years ago through research most people have never heard of. It sends a signal that wakes that protein back up. Ten seconds. That's all."
I looked at her. "Is this a joke?"
She smiled. "Just try it."
I almost didn't. It seemed too simple. Too quiet. Nothing about it looked like something that could help a woman who had just forgotten her great-grandson's name in front of her entire family.
But I had nothing left to lose.
I placed the headphones on. And I don't know how to explain what happened. I just know that everything got quiet. Not outside. Inside. The noise that had been running in my head for months, the worry, the fog, the constant reaching for things that weren't there anymore, it all went still.
That night I slept deeply. No tossing. No spiraling thoughts. Just peace.
The next morning I remembered something small. The name of my third-grade teacher. Then a recipe I hadn't made in decades. Then my neighbor's birthday, one I thought I had forgotten forever. At first it seemed random. Until it kept happening.
Day after day, something new came back online. 🙏
By the end of the week I called my sister and we talked for nearly an hour. I didn't lose my train of thought once. I didn't pause. I didn't fumble. My mind felt awake.
I kept listening every night. Ten seconds. That's all. It became my ritual. My reset.
My posture changed. My energy lifted. My confidence returned. I spoke clearer. Looked people in the eye again. I started sleeping through the night. Reading again, and actually remembering what I read.
My daughter said, "Mom… you haven't been this alive since I was a kid." 😭
And then one Sunday, a few months later, I was holding baby James at a family dinner. My grandson walked over and said, "He loves you, Mom. He always calms down when you hold him."
I looked down at that little face. And I remembered his name. His birthday. The story his father told me about picking it. Every detail. Clear as glass.
And I realized something in that moment. God doesn't close doors without opening others. Sometimes the opening is so quiet you almost miss it. But if you're paying attention, if you're brave enough to try something when you have no reason left to believe… the fog lifts. And you remember not just names and dates. You remember who you are.
Some things find you exactly when you need them. I believe this found me. 🙏
If you've felt the fog… if you've watched yourself fading… if you've seen pity in the eyes of people who used to look at you with respect…
Watch the video. You won't find it through a search. Things like this have a way of disappearing quietly, and I don't know how long it stays up.
But if it's still there when you tap below, don't wait. You've waited long enough.
👉 Tap below to see if it's still available.
It brought me back to my family. It brought me back to myself.
Maybe it'll bring you back too. God bless you. 🙏

The difference between a good day and a stiff one can be measured in millimeters—the space between two bones.

Most advice stops at “wear and tear.” Useful, but not complete. What sits between those bones matters. It isn’t empty. 

It’s a thick, protective fluid—many experts call it your joint jelly. When that jelly is thick, parts glide. 

When it thins with age, three ordinary problems line up: more rubbing, less nourishment for cartilage, and an easier path for inflammatory proteins. 

That’s a tidy explanation for stairs that feel taller, lids that feel tighter, and mornings that feel heavier at 60+.

There is a article that explains this plainly. No scare language. 

No magic. Dr. Mark Weis—physician, author, and former U.S. Army doctor—uses simple diagrams to show how joint fluid works and a 10‑second habit you can do at home to support it daily. 

He also discusses research that challenges the “wear‑and‑tear only” story and points to what happens inside the joint as we age.

A brief, honest interruption: when I found this article, I paid $27 to watch it. You can watch it free until midnight tonight. Tap Learn More now and hold your spot.

Inside, you’ll see why an Ivy‑League–linked look at ancient knees raised questions about the old theory. You’ll see hyaluronan—the molecule that helps keep joint jelly thick—and what tends to happen when it declines. 

You’ll learn a practical sequence you can do at home in ten seconds. And you’ll understand why popular ingredients like glucosamine and chondroitin may disappoint many people (based on studies cited in the article).

You’ll also meet a patented European ingredient—Mobilee® (80 mg) which, in the studies cited, was associated with higher hyaluronan levels in joint fluid and early perceived improvements that continued over time. 

There’s a section on pairing this approach with a targeted French maritime pine antioxidant—plus ginger, boswellia, and BioPerine®—presented as a way to speed the perception of comfort and enhance absorption. It’s all laid out without fanfare, which is refreshing.

And then there’s Yuzurihara, a remote Japanese village where many older adults still farm for hours. Their routines—and even a purple staple food you’ll see in the talk—help illustrate why “less scrape, more glide” is a sensible goal.

If you prefer straight answers to loud promises, this will suit you. 

We can’t promise to turn back the clock. We can show you how the mechanism works and what to try, so you can judge with your own body and your own timetable. Results vary. But when joint jelly has body, everyday movement often feels smoother. That’s the point.

Think of the practical wins people 60+ often report after applying what they learn: steadier steps on stairs, fewer “stuck” mornings, surer hands with jars and buttons, walks that feel like walks again. Modest gains, meaningful life.

Reminder: I paid $27 to watch. Your access is free until 11:59 tonight. Tap Learn More now (or use the link in the description) to watch the presentation while it’s open.

• the what (a 10‑second daily habit you can actually do),�

• the when (what timeline to expect),�

• and the how (why Mobilee® 80 mg and French maritime pine are discussed in the plan).

If you’ve tried heat, ice, lists, and a shelf of bottles, it may be time to start where movement starts—the fluid that lets cartilage slide.

I built someone a full funnel for free.

Not a template. Not a swipe file. A real funnel, recorded a full Loom walkthrough, explained the strategy, the why, all of it.

This person has never run a funnel. Never talked to a marketing agency. The most advanced thing they've ever done online is pay someone to put them on Google Maps. They had no idea what affiliate marketing was, no idea what a VSL was, no concept of what it costs to run real ad spend. Nothing.

They came to me asking for help and said we could talk money later. And I said yes because that's just who I am. I root for the underdog because I've been the underdog. I know what it feels like to wake up every day thinking about the people who believed in you and not wanting to let them down. No one handed me anything. Not once. So when someone is starting from zero and genuinely trying, I'm going to show up.

He never opened the Loom. And that shit irked me.

To the point where I decided, you know what, this is now free for everybody. Especially if you're in the financial sector, you can take advantage of this for a fact. ad_creative_bodies:
I stopped counting what the Shopify store cost me. That's not even the part of this I want to talk about.

I'm Mike, 41, freelance developer in Finland. One client has bought 7.5 hours of my day for years now.

Wake up at 6. Coffee. An hour on whatever side project was alive that month before the workday started. Dev work 8 to 4:30, fully booked, someone else's priorities the whole stretch. Family time after that, the only part of the day that wasn't for sale. Then back at it, 7 to 9, most nights, on the thing that was supposed to eventually replace the 7.5 hours.

The Shopify supplement store is the one I actually stopped counting on. Enough that I don't add it up anymore. That's the number that made me stop and ask what I was actually doing with the evenings I didn't have to give away.

Before that: Amazon FBA, private label and wholesale both, inventory sitting in a warehouse I never saw. ClickBank affiliate campaigns that spent money faster than they made it. Different platforms, different products, same result. None of them failed because I didn't try. They failed because each one still needed to be built from nothing, by me, on top of the 7.5 hours already gone.

I found Greg a few years back through a PDF farming course, random IG ad, don't even remember which one. What kept me around wasn't the course. It was how much support he actually gave after I'd paid, which is rarer than it should be. When he built the AI Influencer model, I didn't need convincing on whether he was real. Just whether the model itself made sense for someone with my actual hours.

What's different mechanically: the build isn't mine to do. The AI influencer, the product, the sales page, the backend, someone else builds all of it first. My part is posting a few short AI videos a day, under twenty minutes. Not a funnel to design from scratch at 8pm again.

The part I didn't expect: nothing stops you from building your own product later and running it through the exact same model. Same influencer, same posting system, your own thing to sell instead of theirs. That's what actually stops this from being just one offer. There's no ceiling built into the model itself, only into how far you take it.

I'm not going to tell you I've cracked it. I haven't been doing this long enough to say that honestly, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I can tell you: this is the first one where the 7 to 9 block isn't spent building infrastructure from zero. That's the actual difference. Whether it becomes more than that is still being written.

If you're in the same 7.5-hours-gone-already spot, this is what I actually looked at before deciding it was worth the evenings.
ad_creative_link_titles: The 7 to 9 block

En el marketing de afiliados hay dos tipos de personas: los que intentan aparentar éxito bailando en redes sociales... y los que llevan 20 años generando comisiones reales en silencio.

En el mercado anglosajón se les conoce como "Afiliados Ocultos".

Uno de sus mayores referentes es un veterano hispano radicado en Estados Unidos: galardonado en el Hall of Fame de ClickBank, miembro élite de Digistore24 y con récords oficiales de más de $120,000 USD en comisiones en JVZoo.

Durante dos décadas operó tras bambalinas, demostrando que para vender productos digitales a nivel global no se necesita ser influencer, ni crear contenido diario, ni perseguir amigos y familiares.

Su verdadero poder radica en un sistema codificado de tráfico directo y activos automatizados que hoy enseña a través de su metodología Digital Bootcamp.

En la redacción de Clickompro publicamos un informe especial analizando la identidad de este veterano, su sistema paso a paso y los resultados reales que produce este modelo.

Toca el botón de abajo para ver el caso de estudio completo y acceder a la presentación oficial en video.

ad_creative_bodies:
I stopped counting what the Shopify store cost me. That's not even the part of this I want to talk about.

I'm Mike, 41, freelance developer in Finland. One client has bought 7.5 hours of my day for years now.

Wake up at 6. Coffee. An hour on whatever side project was alive that month before the workday started. Dev work 8 to 4:30, fully booked, someone else's priorities the whole stretch. Family time after that, the only part of the day that wasn't for sale. Then back at it, 7 to 9, most nights, on the thing that was supposed to eventually replace the 7.5 hours.

The Shopify supplement store is the one I actually stopped counting on. Enough that I don't add it up anymore. That's the number that made me stop and ask what I was actually doing with the evenings I didn't have to give away.

Before that: Amazon FBA, private label and wholesale both, inventory sitting in a warehouse I never saw. ClickBank affiliate campaigns that spent money faster than they made it. Different platforms, different products, same result. None of them failed because I didn't try. They failed because each one still needed to be built from nothing, by me, on top of the 7.5 hours already gone.

I found Greg a few years back through a PDF farming course, random IG ad, don't even remember which one. What kept me around wasn't the course. It was how much support he actually gave after I'd paid, which is rarer than it should be. When he built the AI Influencer model, I didn't need convincing on whether he was real. Just whether the model itself made sense for someone with my actual hours.

What's different mechanically: the build isn't mine to do. The AI influencer, the product, the sales page, the backend, someone else builds all of it first. My part is posting a few short AI videos a day, under twenty minutes. Not a funnel to design from scratch at 8pm again.

The part I didn't expect: nothing stops you from building your own product later and running it through the exact same model. Same influencer, same posting system, your own thing to sell instead of theirs. That's what actually stops this from being just one offer. There's no ceiling built into the model itself, only into how far you take it.

I'm not going to tell you I've cracked it. I haven't been doing this long enough to say that honestly, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I can tell you: this is the first one where the 7 to 9 block isn't spent building infrastructure from zero. That's the actual difference. Whether it becomes more than that is still being written.

If you're in the same 7.5-hours-gone-already spot, this is what I actually looked at before deciding it was worth the evenings.
ad_creative_link_titles: The 7 to 9 block

Every guru selling you an affiliate course right now has a dirty little secret.

Their own ads are running on a platform that's eating them alive.

Ask to see their ad account. Not a screenshot from 2021. This week's.

They get very quiet.

Because most of them are still on Facebook. Paying $150 CPMs. Losing accounts on a Tuesday morning. And teaching you to do the same.

My name is Thomas Owen.

I'm an affiliate. Have been for 7 years.

Eight figures in commissions.

ClickBank Diamond in 2022. And 2023. And 2024.

BuyGoods Legends. MaxWeb Gold Partner.

Not agency money. Not client money. My money, on my own campaigns, with my own neck on the line.

And here's my confession.

I was the Facebook guy.

Almost all of it came from one traffic source.

I've done a $203,988 day on Facebook.

I've also lost $97,000 in a couple of hours on Facebook.

So when I tell you where I'd put my next thousand dollars today, understand it isn't sour grapes.

It's not Facebook.

Here's what happened to it.

A few years ago I was running US weight loss traffic at $30 to $40 CPMs.

Today I'd be lucky to see anything under $150.

Thousands of new affiliates piled in.

Telehealth started dumping billions into the auction.

Ecom came back with a vengeance.

Then Andromeda landed and most affiliates never adapted.

That's before the account shutdowns. The profile sweeps. The selfie verifications.

But the CPMs aren't what made me move.

It was this.

You can do everything right, build something profitable, and lose the whole thing because a review bot didn't like your landing page.

You cannot build a business on rented land where the landlord changes the locks at random.

So a few months ago I went looking for somewhere else to run.

And I found it hiding in plain sight.

Newsbreak.

I know. It's no secret. It's been around for years. You might even have an account sitting there right now.

But almost nobody is running it properly.

And that's exactly why it works.

While everyone else is bidding against telehealth budgets and 40,000 dropshippers...

I'm getting traffic that holds up against Facebook quality, at a fraction of the CPM.

Offers I could never push past 2% on Facebook are converting at 4 and 5%.

I haven't lost a single account. And I'm not running gentle campaigns.

Here are the last two days. Straight from the Newsbreak dashboard.

Sunday: $660.97 spent. 31 sales. $2,325 back.

Monday: $1,902.40 spent. 61 sales. $4,575 back.

Now here's the part every guru skips.

Ad platforms are famously generous about counting their own conversions.

So I pulled the same two days from my tracker. Different system. Different company. Counting independently.

Sunday: 32.

Monday: 63.

Within a couple of sales of each other, both days.

That's what makes a screenshot worth looking at.

And it isn't just me.

Priank hit his first $4,500 day four weeks in. Not four years.

Sudip's first profitable day came off an $82.03 test. $259.40 back.

Eighty two dollars.

Right now the whole thing averages about $1,000 a day.

Now, I'm not going to tell you which offer it is.

Not because I'm precious about it. Because the moment I name it on a call with a few hundred affiliates, it's dead inside a week. For me and for you.

What I will show you is how I picked it. The criteria I run every offer through before it gets a dollar of Newsbreak budget.

And the campaign structure. The same structure I run on every Newsbreak campaign I have.

The offer changes. The structure doesn't. That's the part worth $47.

On Wednesday at 1pm ET / 6pm UK, I'm going to share my screen and show you how the whole thing is built, live.

Not a slideshow. Not theory.

The offers that crush on Newsbreak, and the ones that quietly eat your test budget and die.

The exact campaign structure.

What a winning ad looks like next to a losing one.

Testing through to scaling.

And the tracker check, so you always know when a platform is lying to you.

Then you keep the folder.

Every setting, the offer criteria, the launch checklist. You point your own Claude or ChatGPT at it and it builds the campaign with you.

It's $47.

One payment. No bumps. No upsells. Nothing pitched on the call.

Full refund any time before we go live. Email me. No form, no questions.

Doors close when we go live.

Click below to reserve your seat.

Look, I know how this reads. Another traffic source. Another workshop.

But I'm showing you two days of real numbers from two separate systems.

And I'm running it live on Wednesday.

You'll know inside 60 minutes whether this is for you.
ad_creative_link_descriptions: Sixty to ninety minutes over my shoulder. How I pick offers, the structure, the ads, the tracker check. Then you keep the folder.
ad_creative_link_titles: Watch Me Build A $1k A Day Affiliate Campaign Live...

ad_creative_bodies:
কানাডার এক ভাই, দুইটা চাকরি, মাসে ৬,৭০০ ডলার — আর তাঁর প্রথম goal হলো মাসে ১,৫০০ ডলার আয় করা। সেই onboarding call নিয়েই আজকের podcast episode।

হিসাবটা আমি দুইবার দেখলাম।

মানুষটা বেশি আয় করতে চান না।

তিনি কম আয় করতে চান। 😐

এক

প্রথমে ভাবলাম শুনতে ভুল করেছি।

তারপর বুঝলাম, ভুল শুনিনি।

তাঁর একটা রাতের চাকরি আছে। সপ্তাহে তিন রাত। মাসে ১,৫০০ ডলার।

তিনি ওই চাকরিটা ছাড়তে চান।

কিন্তু ১,৫০০ ডলার তো লাগবেই। তাই তিনি চান — অন্য কোথাও থেকে ঠিক ১,৫০০ ডলার আসুক।

লাভ শূন্য। হিসাব সমান।

তিনি শুধু রাতগুলো ফেরত চান।

দুই

আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, main job-টা কেমন?

বললেন, main job ঠিক আছে। মাসে ৪,২০০ ডলার। নভেম্বর মাসটা একটু busy, বাকি বছর chill.

আমি বললাম — এই income-এর জন্য এই পরিমাণ শ্রম আর সময়, doesn't make any sense to me.

তিনি বললেন, "মানে... তাও তো total ৬,৭০০।"

তারপর নিজেই থামলেন।

"Sorry. Makes no sense." 🙂

মানুষ নিজের হিসাব নিজেই ভেঙে ফেলে। আমাকে কিছু করতে হয় না।

তিন

তারপর তিনি এমন একটা কথা বললেন, যেটা শুনে আমি এক মুহূর্ত চুপ করে ছিলাম।

"আমি job-এ গিয়ে break time নিয়ে দেড় দুই ঘন্টা ঘুমায়া থাকি।"

রাতের ডিউটি করে সকালে main job. Main job-এর break room-এ ঘুম।

একটা চাকরি খেয়ে ফেলছে আরেকটা চাকরিকে।

দুইটা চাকরি মিলে খেয়ে ফেলছে মানুষটাকে। 😔

চার

আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, "next six months যদি এভাবেই চলে, কোন change না হয়, কী হবে?"

তিনি বললেন, ছয় মাস চালিয়ে নিতে পারবেন — যদি জানেন যে ছয় মাস পরে কিছু একটা আছে।

তারপর একটু থেমে বললেন:

"But if nothing changes — এটা আমাকে শেষ করে দিবে।"

আমি বললাম, "ভাষায় describe করেন। আমি লিখব।"

তিনি করলেন। Health. Family time. Social life. আর main job.

চারটা শব্দ। চারটাই তাঁর।

পাঁচ

তাঁর স্ত্রীও এই রাতের চাকরিটা নিয়ে depressed. রাতে বাসায় একা থাকতে হয়।

আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, বাচ্চা আছে?

বললেন, না। এখনো না।

"আলহামদুলিল্লাহ" বলেই বললেন।

মানুষ যখন "এখনো না" বলে আলহামদুলিল্লাহ যোগ করে, তখন বুঝতে হয় সে অপেক্ষা করছে। 🤲

ছয়

এবার পিছনের গল্পটা।

এই ভাই কিন্তু হঠাৎ করে online-এ আসেননি। তিনি চেষ্টা করেছিলেন। অনেক চেষ্টা।

Amazon FBA. ছয়-সাত মাস সময় নিয়ে শিখেছেন। Product research, পুরো system কীভাবে কাজ করে — সব।

তারপর business দাঁড় করিয়েছেন। প্রায় ৫০ হাজার ডলারের sales.

USA-তে warehouse. সব online. সব চলছিল।

সাত

তারপর চাকরি আর business একসাথে চালাতে গিয়ে সময় দিতে পারলেন না।

কিছু product এদিক-ওদিক হলো। Customer complain করল।

Amazon account ban করে দিল। ⚠️

আমি ভেবেছিলাম গল্পটা এখানেই শেষ।

গল্পটা এখানে শুরু।

আট

তিনি বললেন, "আপনি যা earn করবেন — account যদি block হয়ে যায়, you cannot take that money. Never."

আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, টাকাটা তো আপনার?

"হ্যাঁ, আমার মানি। কিন্তু আমি নিতে পারব না। Because account blocked."

Terms and conditions-এ লেখাই আছে। ব্যবসা শুরুর দিনেই আপনি রাজি হয়ে এসেছেন।

কলের মধ্যেই শব্দটা তৈরি হলো — legal robbery. 🧾

শব্দটা কারও একার না। দুইজনেরই।

নয়

Loss কত?

১৫ থেকে ২০ হাজার ডলার।

Product গুলো এখনো আমেরিকায় পড়ে আছে। কানাডায় আনতে হলে দুই-তিন হাজার ডলার tariff.

তিনি বললেন, "আমি আর কোন টাকা invest করতে চাই না। So I lost everything."

দশ

তারপর আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, প্রথম টাকাটা এসেছিল কোথা থেকে?

তিনি খুব সহজভাবে বললেন — student থাকতে food delivery করতেন। সেই টাকা জমিয়ে business শুরু করেছিলেন।

আমি কিছু বললাম না।

Food delivery-র সঞ্চয়। আমেরিকার warehouse-এ আটকে থাকা কার্টন। আর terms and conditions-এর একটা লাইন।

তিনজনের দেখা হলো না কোনোদিন।

এগারো

Loss-এর পরের ছয়-সাত মাস নিয়ে তিনি যা বললেন, সেটা টাকার হিসাব না।

"আমি literally six seven months এত depressed ছিলাম। আমার শরীরের weight বেড়ে গেছে। আমার চেহারার অবস্থা উল্টাপাল্টা হয়ে গেছে।"

"প্রতিদিন একটা tension-এ আমি থাকতাম — কী হয় না হয়, কী হয় না হয়।"

ব্যবসার loss শরীরে লেখা থাকে। Bank statement-এ না। 💔

বারো

Account একবার suspend হলে আর কী করার আছে?

তিনি বললেন, নিজের নামে আর কখনো account খোলা যাবে না। অন্য কারও নামে খুলতে হবে।

"এই risk, এই ঝামেলা আমি আর নিতেই চাই না।"

আমি বললাম, ঠিক আছে। এই part শেষ। এটা আমরা delete করে দিতে পারি।

Whiteboard-এ Amazon-এর ঘরটা কেটে দিলাম। মানুষটার মুখটা হালকা হয়ে গেল।

কিছু জিনিস কেটে দেওয়ার জন্যই লেখা হয়। ✂️

তেরো

Whiteboard-এ তখন একটা জিনিসই রইল — tax.

গত বছর তিনি tax filing-এর কাজ শিখেছেন। Seasonal. দুই-তিন মাসের কাজ।

প্রথম season-এ ১৭০ জন client.

তিনি বললেন, "যেটা আমি কখনো চিন্তাও করি নাই যে আমি পাব।"

আর কাজটা তাঁর ভালো লাগে। অফিসে বসে করেন, বাসায় বসে করেন। যেখানে ইচ্ছা।

চৌদ্দ

আমি তিনটা জিনিস আলাদা করে দেখালাম।

এক, এটা seasonal — মানে short term. দুই-তিন মাসে যদি যথেষ্ট আসে, বাকি বছর নিয়ে ভাবতে হয় না।

দুই, নতুন হয়েও ১৭০ client — এটা কম কথা না।

তিন — তিনি charge করেন lawyer-দের অর্ধেক।

আমি বললাম, এটা massive red flag. 🚩

কম দাম মানে বেশি client না। কম দাম মানে মানুষ ভাবে, "এত সস্তা কেন?"

পনেরো

আরও একটা জিনিস বললাম, যেটা আমি সবাইকে বলি না।

Amazon তাঁকে anxiety দিয়েছে।

Tax-এর কাজটা তাঁকে fun দিয়েছে।

Part-time রাতের চাকরিটা তাঁর mental health, physical health, social health — সব ভেঙে দিচ্ছে।

আর tax-এর কাজটা তাঁকে আনন্দ দিচ্ছে।

পাশাপাশি না লিখলে এগুলো চোখে পড়ে না। এমনি এমনি ভাবলে কখনো আসে না। 📝

ষোল

তারপর তিনি খুব সৎ একটা কথা বললেন।

"এছাড়া আর কোন way তো আমার কাছে নাই।"

আমি বললাম, way আছে। এইতো আছে। আপনি শুধু জানেন না।

"আপনি জানেন না — how. Period. আপনি just জানেন না how."

আগে এটা accept করে নিতে হয়: আমি জানি না।

মানুষ "আমি জানি না" বলতে যত দেরি করে, শেখা তত দেরিতে শুরু হয়।

সতেরো

তাঁর প্রশ্ন ছিল তিনটা। আমি whiteboard-এ লিখে ফেললাম।

এক — What are the products?

দুই — affiliate ছাড়া আর কী কী earning-এর way আছে?

তিন — social media দিয়ে tax-এর কাজটা scale করা যায় কীভাবে?

Product-এর উত্তরে যাওয়ার আগে তিনি হঠাৎ থামিয়ে দিলেন।

"একটা question মাঝখানে — sorry. Dropshipping হালাল না কেন?"

আঠারো

আমি বললাম, খুব সহজ কথা।

যে জিনিস আপনার কাছে নেই, আপনার inventory-তে নেই, সেটার payment আপনি নিজে collect করতে পারেন না।

Affiliate marketing-এ আপনি payment collect করছেন না। Owner করছে।

আপনি শুধু মানুষকে পথ দেখাচ্ছেন। 🤍

ওলামাদের মধ্যে কোন কোন শর্তে কী হবে — সেই বিস্তারিত বিতর্কে আমি যাইনি। যতটুকু আমি জানি ততটুকুই বলেছি।

আর একটা কথা বলেছি, যেটা অনেকের ভালো লাগবে না:

"Amazon affiliate is the worst thing ever."

উনিশ

Product কেন নিজে বানাচ্ছি না — সেই প্রশ্নেরও উত্তর দিলাম।

আমি যখন মাসে একটা-দুইটা product launch করতাম, প্রতিটা launch-এ ৬৮টা step ছিল।

তিনি অবাক হয়ে জিজ্ঞেস করলেন, "কয়টা step?"

৬৮।

১০০ হাজার ডলারের launch তখন normal ব্যাপার ছিল। ৫০ হাজার, ১০০ হাজার — normal.

কিন্তু ওই জায়গায় পৌঁছাতে বছরের পর বছর লেগেছে। একদিনে হয়নি।

Copywriting, graphic design, funnel design — প্রত্যেকটা আলাদা জিনিস। একজন beginner-এর জন্য প্রত্যেকটাই নতুন।

তাই beginner-এর জন্য সবচেয়ে সহজ দরজাটা affiliate.

বিশ

Product-এর উত্তর দিলাম তিনটা option-এ।

এক — আমাদের নিজেদের program. আপনি চান বা না চান, আপনার জন্য ready করে দেওয়া থাকবে, free. ৫০০ ডলার commission. কোনো obligation নেই।

দুই — digital marketplace. JVZoo, DigiStore24, ClickBank. Top-level product, ৩০% থেকে ৭০% পর্যন্ত commission. Product কিনতে হয় না।

তিন — your own offer. আপনার tax offer. অন্য যেকোনো offer.

"You have three options. Not one. All options."

আর funnel? Funnel আমরা বানিয়ে দেব। তিনটারই।

আমাদের নিজেদের বানানো software আর team-ই ওই ৯৯% technical কাজ করে দেয়। 🛠️

একুশ

Funnel জিনিসটা তিনি ঠিক ধরতে পারছিলেন না। তাই আমি McDonald's-এ চলে গেলাম।

জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, McDonald's টাকা কামায় কোথা থেকে?

তিনি বললেন, franchise থেকে। Consumer থেকে।

আমি বললাম, জিলাপির প্যাঁচ দিবেন না। 😄

আসল উত্তর — real estate.

তারপর franchise-এর ভিতরটা: ওদের ice cream machine ব্যবহার করতে হবে, ওদের maintenance guy ডাকতে হবে, ওদের uniform পরতে হবে, ওদের খাবারই বেচতে হবে।

আর সেই maintenance guy কোনোদিন এসে ঠিক করবে না। আপনার ice cream machine সবসময় broken থাকবে।

আপনি ওদের funnel-এর ভিতরে ঢুকে গেছেন।

বাইশ

Supermarket-এর গল্পটাও বললাম।

সব জিনিসের দাম কম রাখলেন — দুই দিনে broke.

সব জিনিসের দাম বেশি রাখলেন — দুই দিনে customer শেষ।

ওরা এত সামান্য করে দাম বাড়ায়-কমায় যে আপনার চোখ ধরতেই পারে না। Sale-এর তাকের দিকে হেঁটে যেতে যেতে আপনি আরও পাঁচটা তাকের পাশ দিয়ে যান।

আর আপনি বলতেও পারবেন না, "আমি শুধু সস্তা জিনিসটা এই দোকান থেকে কিনব, আরেকটা সস্তা জিনিসের জন্য আরেক দোকানে যাব।"

দূর। সময় নাই। Energy নাই। চল বাসায় যাই।

ওদের funnel complete. 🛒

যারা funnel চিন্তা করে না, তারা সারাজীবন পেটে-ভাতে থাকে।

তেইশ

তারপর আমি তিনটা P লিখলাম।

Product. People. Place (বা platform)।

Product আছে — তিনটা option।

Place আছে — website, funnel, সব আমরা করে দিচ্ছি।

বাকি থাকল People.

আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, "আপনি কি এখন on demand ১০০০ visitor কোথাও send করতে পারবেন?"

তিনি বললেন, "না।"

চব্বিশ

তখন আমি screen share করলাম।

তিন ঘণ্টা আগে publish করা একটা video. ১.২K views.

আরেকটা — তিন ঘণ্টা আগে। ১.২K.

আমি বললাম, ভাই, I know how to get traffic. Traffic মানে হচ্ছে I have customers. People.

আমার people আছে, কাজেই আমার টাকা আছে।

আপনার নাই।

So your next step — people.

আর কিছু চিন্তা করার দরকার নাই। Clarity. একটা tension শেষ। 🎯

পঁচিশ

People কোথায়? Social media-তে।

Short video যখন এসেছিল, মানুষ পাগলের মতো short video দেখত। আমরা তখন hundreds of thousands of leads পেয়েছি।

ঘুম থেকে উঠে email check করতাম — কয়েক পাতা email. সব নতুন lead. একটা video viral হয়ে গেছে।

কিন্তু সেই সময় বদলে গেছে।

এখন শুধু short video না — text কাজ করে, image কাজ করে, thread post খুব ভালো কাজ করে।

Adaptability. গতকাল যেটা true ছিল, আজকে সেটা true নাই।

আর Facebook — পৃথিবীর তিন নম্বর crowded website. আপনার aged traffic প্রায় সবই ওখানে। 📱

ছাব্বিশ

তারপর তিনি আসল প্রশ্নটা করলেন। যেটা সবাই করে।

"আমার next step কী? কবে থেকে start করতে পারব? এই কাজটা নিজে হাতে না দিলে confidence-টা ওভাবে আসে না।"

এই প্রশ্নটার জন্যই আমরা একটা জিনিস বানিয়েছি।

কানাডারই আরেক ভাই একদিন বললেন — "ভাই, আমি কিচ্ছু বুঝতেছি না। কোর্সের A to Z কিচ্ছু বুঝি নাই। কোনো guidance নাই, এরপর আমি কী করব?"

৬০০ member. ৬০০ testimonial. আর একজন ভাই বসে আছেন, মাথায় কিছু ঢুকছে না।

আমি বললাম, দুই-তিন দিন সবুর করেন। 🙂

সাতাশ

আমরা একটা AI Coach বানালাম। প্রথম version আরও simple ছিল।

উনি দেখে বললেন, "কী দিছেন এটা? ChatGPT-ই তো করতে পারে।"

আমি বললাম, ভাই — ChatGPT যদি করতেই পারে, তাহলে আপনি ব্যবহার করেন না কেন?

তারপর আমরা fine tune করলাম। Negative feedback, positive feedback — সব নিয়েছি।

এখন AI Coach ১৪ দিন ধরে প্রতিদিন ছোট ছোট task দেয়। Overwhelm না করে। প্রথম দিন একটা thread post লেখো। তৃতীয় দিনে একটা video করো। কিছু একটা শিখে এসে report করো।

আর আপনি যদি প্রতিদিন topic বদলান, সে বলবে — "Why are you changing topic? You're not learning anything."

আমাদের পুরো business feedback-এর উপর দাঁড়ানো। Software-ও। 🧩

আটাশ

আরেকজন member ছিলেন, যিনি ঘুম থেকে উঠে আমাকে চার-পাঁচটা লম্বা প্রশ্ন পাঠালেন।

প্রথমটা refund নিয়ে। দ্বিতীয়টা refund. তৃতীয়টা refund. চতুর্থটাও refund.

আমি রাগ করিনি। আমি agent দিয়ে analyse করলাম — মানুষটার মনের ভিতরে কী চলছে।

মানুষ আগে টাকা ফেরত পাওয়ার রাস্তাটা দেখে নিতে চায়। তারপর হাঁটে।

দোষ দেওয়া যায় না। অনেকেই আগে খেয়েছে।

ঊনত্রিশ

তারপর তাঁকে আমাদের agent গুলো দেখালাম।

Find My Social Pitch. Build My Brand Kit. Write My First Post. Find My Buyers.

Social pitch জিনিসটা কী? কেউ যখন জিজ্ঞেস করে "আপনি কী করেন" — প্রশ্নটা আসলে "What do you do for a living" না। প্রশ্নটা আসলে "What are you?"

আপনি যদি বলেন "আমার নাম অমুক, আমি অমুক অফিসে চাকরি করি" — কথাটা এমন জায়গায় যাবে যার আগাও নাই, মাথাও নাই। দুইজনই bore হয়ে চলে যাবেন।

Name. Fame. Aim. তিরিশ সেকেন্ড।

আর আমি একটা কথা পরিষ্কার করে বলে দিলাম — নিজেকে কখনো "affiliate marketer" বলবেন না। "Digital marketer"-ও না।

কারণ MLM-রা এই শব্দগুলো নষ্ট করে দিয়েছে। 🙃

ত্রিশ

Write My First Post agent-টা আমি তাঁর সামনেই চালিয়ে দিলাম।

ভিতরে কয়েকটা agent একসাথে কাজ করে। একজন story খোঁজে। একজন লেখে। একজন hook বসায়।

তারপর Truth Critic — যাতে কোথাও hallucination না থাকে।

তারপর Safeguard — যাতে "I help people make six figures in three months" টাইপের উল্টাপাল্টা claim কোথাও না থাকে।

তারপর Polisher.

আমাদের software-এর ভিতরে একটা agent-এর কাজই হলো মিথ্যা ধরা।

আমার মনে হয় এটা আমাদের সবচেয়ে দরকারি feature. ✅

একত্রিশ

তিনি জিজ্ঞেস করলেন, তাহলে আমার কাজটা কী?

আমি বললাম, coordination.

তিনি বললেন, "আমার system-ই আমাকে সবকিছু বের করে দিবে। আমাকে just coordinate করতে হবে।"

Correct. 🎯

মানুষটা দুই ঘণ্টায় জিনিসটা ধরে ফেলেছেন।

বত্রিশ

Camera নিয়ে তাঁর একটা দ্বিধা ছিল। প্রায় সবারই থাকে।

আমি বললাম — camera আছে তো ভালো। কিন্তু don't even think about camera.

Additional hassle না। Additional stress না। Additional anxiety না।

Everything is your story.

আমার নিজের গল্পটাই বললাম। আমার মেয়ে অসুস্থ ছিল। Manager-কে early leave-এর কথা বলেছিলাম। তিনি না বললেন।

আমি resignation দিয়ে দিয়েছিলাম। উনি সেটা reject করেছিলেন।

কিন্তু ওই দিনই আমি বুঝেছিলাম — building another person's dream is not building your dream.

এত বছরের সম্পর্ক, ওরকম position, ওরকম reputation। আর মুখের উপর "না"। 🥀

তেত্রিশ

শেষদিকে তিনি একটা অস্বস্তিকর প্রশ্ন করলেন — যেটা তাঁকেও কেউ করবে।

"মানুষ তো জিজ্ঞেস করবে, তুমি নিজে কত earn করেছ?"

আমি বললাম, সাধারণ মানুষ কী করে জানেন? একটা way বের করে ফেলে বলার জন্য যে "আমি কিছু একটা result পেয়েছি"।

মানুষ তখন ethics চিন্তা করে না।

Stand out করার একটাই উপায় — শক্ত করে বলা:

"I just started. I did not make a single penny yet."

আর চোখের দিকে তাকিয়ে থাকা।

আমি আজকে medical-এ ঢুকলে ছয়-সাত বছর লাগত। Engineering হলে চার বছর। জীবনে সম্পূর্ণ নতুন একটা জিনিস শুরু করেছি।

Of course I did not earn yet।

এটা যদি earn করে ফেলতাম, তাহলে তো এটা get-rich-quick scheme হয়ে যেত। 🙂

চৌত্রিশ

কল শেষে আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, এই call-টাকে পাঁচের মধ্যে কত দেবেন?

তিনি বললেন, আরও কিছু সময় পেলে, আরও কিছু question prepare করতে পারলে ভালো হতো। কিন্তু "five out of five. আমি অনেক satisfied."

আমি বললাম, আমি তো satisfied না। আপনি আমাকে অনেক দুঃখ দিলেন।

তিনি ঘাবড়ে গিয়ে বললেন, "কেন ভাইয়া?"

"আপনি ঢুকছেন affiliate marketing-এ, আর rating দিছেন five। আমার bonus কোথায়?" 😄

পাশ থেকে তাঁর দশ বছরের ছেলে হেসে ফেলল।

আমি বললাম, ঠিক আছে — seven out of five, এই আর কি।

পঁয়ত্রিশ

শেষ প্রশ্নটা ছিল practical.

"Post গুলো কি আমার personal profile থেকে যাবে?"

আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলাম, আপনার existing follower-রা কোথাকার?

বাংলাদেশের।

তাহলে নতুন page করেন। ওদিকে traffic যাওয়ার দরকার নাই। আপনার traffic হবে Canadian, North American.

তিনি বললেন, "লেটস try. প্রথম video হলে আপনাকে send করব।"

আমি বললাম — video-র জন্য অপেক্ষা করার দরকার নাই। Post দিয়ে শুরু করেন।

শুরু করাটাই আসল। বাকিটা সময় করে দেয়। 🌱

ছত্রিশ

আপনিও হয়তো এভাবেই আছেন।

Canada, UK, USA, Australia — যেখানেই থাকুন। একটা চাকরি, নয়তো দুইটা।

হয়তো আপনিও একবার কিছু একটা try করেছিলেন। টাকা গেছে। মন ভেঙেছে। ছয় মাস আর কারও সাথে কথা বলতে ইচ্ছা করেনি।

হয়তো আপনার মনেও প্রশ্ন — "এটা হালাল তো?"

হয়তো আপনিও ভাবেন, "আমার মতো লোকের পক্ষে কি সম্ভব?"
